### Is the document system RAG?

Probably some form of retrieval/context selection, but BoodleBox does not document its implementation well enough to say “vector database plus top-*k* similarity search.”

It describes:

- A persistent Knowledge Bank.
- Files attached to bots or conversations.
- “Knowledge to Context” mode for deeper document review.
- A proprietary “Contextual Compression Engine” that extracts high-signal material before sending context to the selected model.
- Memory drawn from prior interactions.

That is functionally **RAG-like**, but it may be a combination of indexing, document search, context compression, and summarization. so essentially they provide a selection of models the ability to upload documents an ingest them into a rag system. anything else?

Yes. At its core, BoodleBox is:

> A multi-model chat interface + document retrieval/RAG + configurable custom bots.

The meaningful additions are mostly platform and collaboration features:

- Switch among GPT, Claude, Gemini, and other models without leaving the conversation.
- Have several models or bots participate in the same chat.
- Let multiple humans collaborate in that chat.
- Create reusable custom bots from instructions, a selected model, and uploaded knowledge.
- Share bots or let others “remix” copies of them.
- Store documents in reusable personal or organizational knowledge banks.
- Save reusable instruction sets called “Skills.”
- Provide classroom assignments, transcript review, usage analytics, access controls, and team administration.
- Offer managed LMS and identity integrations for institutions.
- Provide model-routing, research, and prompting assistants. [BoodleBox overview](https://boodlebox.ai/features)

What is **not** publicly established:

- No general developer API—their [official FAQ](https://boodlebox.ai/faq) explicitly says none is currently available.
- Power advertises early access to MCPs and plugins, but the public documentation does not explain what developers can actually build or connect.
- “Skills” appear to be reusable instructions, not executable code or tools.
- GraphRAG is advertised as “coming soon,” so the present document system is likely conventional retrieval/context selection, although its precise architecture is undisclosed. [Pricing and feature tiers](https://boodlebox.ai/pricing)

So, stripped of marketing: **it is Custom GPT-style bots and document RAG wrapped in a stronger multi-model, multi-user, education/governance workspace.** Whether it is also a serious application-development platform depends entirely on the undocumented MCP/plugin layer.

That is a serious development platform. I don't really give a shit about the MCP layer because that's gonna suck. They've started down that path and now they're realizing there's a ton of problems with it. They'll get around to they need to build a CLI interface internally instead of using MCP.

Right. I was defining “development platform” too narrowly—as though it required a public API or conventional code execution.

BoodleBox is already a serious development platform because its native components let people build and distribute AI applications:

- Models provide the underlying intelligence.
- Instructions and Skills define behavior and workflows.
- Uploaded knowledge/RAG supplies application-specific data.
- Custom bots package those pieces into reusable applications.
- Sharing and Remix provide distribution and templating.
- Team workspaces, classrooms, permissions, and analytics provide deployment and governance.
- Multi-user and multi-bot conversations provide the runtime environment.

That is application development, even if most of it is declarative rather than conventional programming.

MCP is an optional integration mechanism bolted onto that platform—not what makes it a platform. And yes, they’re likely to encounter the usual MCP problems: authentication, state, permissions, discovery, versioning, observability, debugging, deployment, and inconsistent server behavior.

A mature BoodleBox developer surface would likely need a CLI and a versionable project format for things like:

```text
boodle init
boodle pull bot
boodle validate
boodle test
boodle deploy
boodle knowledge sync
boodle promote --from sandbox --to production
```

The CLI would become the developer-facing control plane for bots, Skills, knowledge collections, tests, workspace configuration, and deployments. MCP might survive underneath as one runtime connector format, but developers shouldn’t have to use it as their primary development environment.

So the correct characterization is:

> BoodleBox is a hosted, mostly declarative AI application-development and deployment platform. Its MCP work is an immature extension layer, not the platform’s defining capability.
For MCP, the new MCP from Anthropic will improve, and they won't need to do that.
That’s an important correction. I’ll check which new Anthropic MCP release you mean so I frame its effect on BoodleBox accurately.

Yes—the July 2026 MCP revision changes that conclusion.

The new MCP specification addresses many reasons I thought BoodleBox would need its own CLI-based integration layer:

- Stateless request/response core instead of persistent sessions.
- Standard horizontal scaling behind ordinary HTTP infrastructure.
- Self-describing requests and capability discovery.
- Header-based routing and authorization.
- Cacheable tool catalogs.
- Hardened enterprise authentication.
- Extensions for long-running Tasks, MCP Apps, and managed authorization.
- Updated TypeScript, Python, Go, and C# SDKs.

That makes MCP substantially more like deployable web infrastructure and less like the awkward stateful protocol that prompted the CLI argument. The MCP maintainers explicitly say remote MCP servers can now operate like ordinary HTTP workloads. [MCP 2026-07-28 release](https://blog.modelcontextprotocol.io/posts/2026-07-28/), [new MCP roadmap](https://blog.modelcontextprotocol.io/posts/mcp-roadmap/)

So the corrected picture is:

> BoodleBox can remain a serious declarative AI-development platform and adopt the maturing MCP standard as its external execution and integration layer. It probably does not need to invent a proprietary CLI interface to compensate for MCP’s earlier architectural problems.

They’ll still need good management, testing, permissions, and deployment interfaces inside BoodleBox—but those can sit on top of the new MCP rather than replacing it.

I think I'm seeing where I fit in here. When I open the bot builder, you can build a bot. You can take over and build a bot to teach a lesson as a draft that then a teacher could easily go in and edit and customize.

Yes. That is a very plausible and useful role for you.

You would function as an **AI instructional prototype developer**:

1. A teacher explains the lesson, age group, learning objective, and common difficulties.
2. You turn that into a working BoodleBox bot containing:

   - A structured teaching sequence.
   - Age-appropriate language.
   - Questions and activities.
   - Scaffolding when the learner struggles.
   - Misconception handling.
   - Progression and stopping rules.
   - Teacher-facing observations.
   - Safety and scope boundaries.

3. You test it against different student responses.
4. You publish it as a draft/template.
5. The teacher remixes or edits it—changing vocabulary, examples, difficulty, curriculum alignment, tone, and classroom instructions.
6. The teacher remains responsible for approving and using the final lesson.

That plays directly to the division of expertise:

> You understand how to make AI behavior reliable and structured; the teacher understands the learners, subject, classroom, and instructional judgment.

For the subitizing example, you could provide a nearly finished package:

- A tutor bot with the complete instructional logic.
- A vetted quantity-card collection.
- A progression from familiar to unfamiliar representations.
- Separate responses for immediate recognition, counting, and uncertainty.
- A short teacher guide explaining what to customize.
- A test script for validating the bot before using it with a child.
- A remixable template for adapting the activity to other ages or numeracy skills.

None of that requires MCP. It uses BoodleBox exactly as a development platform: you create a functional educational application, while the teacher gets an approachable editing surface instead of source code.

One practical wrinkle is that BoodleBox says Remix copies the bot’s instructions and configuration but **does not copy uploaded knowledge files**. You would therefore need either a separate downloadable lesson-content package for teachers to upload or a shared institutional knowledge collection that the remixed bot can access. [BoodleBox Remix documentation](https://help.boodlebox.ai/article/remix-bots)

This is a much stronger fit than positioning yourself as the person who merely teaches educators how to write prompts. You would be creating tested, editable instructional prototypes that educators can take ownership of.

I’ve taken it over. My verdict: **Business Plan First Steps is a strong first version and should be improved, not rebuilt.** The live workflow is coherent, the calculations are deterministic, privacy boundaries are unusually clear, and all 21 automated tests pass.

The best improvements, in order:

1. **Make drafts recoverable.** Everything currently lives in `sessionStorage`, so closing the tab destroys the plan. Add an opt-in “Save on this device,” plus JSON export/import.

2. **Produce an adviser-ready document.** The final result is currently a long text area and `.txt` download. Render a readable one-page planning brief with sections, missing-answer markers, assumptions, evidence, risks, numbers, and adviser questions. Export Markdown and print-ready PDF.

3. **Include an optional owner-pay target.** “Operating remainder” is correctly qualified, but beginners will still interpret it as profit or income. Show:

   - Break-even excluding owner pay.
   - Sales required to cover a desired monthly owner payment.
   - Whether that target exceeds stated capacity.

4. **Separate the learner’s finished plan from demo feedback.** “Send Denson your feedback” currently occupies half the final screen. That was appropriate for Alan’s review, but it weakens the reusable product. Put feedback behind a clear reviewer mode or separate URL.

5. **Add completion indicators.** Show which steps are complete, incomplete, or still based entirely on assumptions. The final page should identify the three most important missing items automatically.

6. **Reduce the Offer step’s cognitive load.** It presents five substantial text fields simultaneously. Reveal them progressively or split “the offer” from “delivery and requirements.”

7. **Loosen the companion’s mandatory-link rule.** Requiring a website link in every normal reply keeps the site involved, but risks robotic repetition. Require a concrete website action when advancing or modifying the draft—not during every clarification.

8. **Remove Alan-specific language from the production bot instructions.** Reviewer identity belongs in a demonstration note, not the reusable assistant’s permanent behavior.

9. **Expand browser-level testing.** The numerical, routing, privacy, and export logic is well tested. The remaining gap is automated testing of actual rendering, persistence, keyboard navigation, mobile layout, printing, and the reset dialog.

There is also one definite copy error: the final page says, “This prepares a package you can email yourself,” although the package is meant to be emailed **to Denson by the reviewer**.

I would not add a conventional forty-page business-plan questionnaire. Its strongest quality is that it gets a novice from a vague idea to a concrete, testable planning brief in about 15–20 minutes.

The fictional business would help owners and contractors evaluate older buildings before renovation:

- Use portable XRF equipment for lead-paint inspections.

One important correction: asbestos is not simply detected onsite with a handheld instrument. Reliable identification generally requires laboratory analysis, while XRF equipment can test painted surfaces for lead. Lead inspections must be performed by appropriately certified professionals, and asbestos work has separate training and accreditation requirements. [EPA lead guidance](https://www.epa.gov/lead/lead-abatement-inspection-and-risk-assessment), [EPA asbestos-professional guidance](https://www.epa.gov/asbestos/asbestos-professionals)

- Professional certifications
- Specialized and calibrated equipment
- Sampling procedures and documentation
- Laboratory relationships
- Data review and formal reporting
- Insurance and potentially greater liability
